text: Earlier in this path you covered platform engineering: internal platform teams build self-service golden paths, so provisioning a service, a database, or a CI/CD pipeline comes with sensible defaults already wired in — logging, deployment, autoscaling, secrets management — without every product team needing deep infra expertise of its own. That's the paved road. This lesson is about what's genuinely different between that job and SRE's job, and why the two end up working so closely together once an organization is running at the scale this chapter has been describing.

It's tempting to treat SRE and platform engineering as two names for the same team, but they have different jobs even sitting close together. Platform engineering builds and maintains the paved road itself — the tools, templates, and self-service systems. SRE is responsible for the reliability of what actually runs on that road: SLOs, the error budget policy from Lesson 2, incident response, and the toil-reduction discipline from Lesson 3. A platform team can ship a beautifully designed paved road, and a service running on it can still have a terrible SLO, because reliability depends on how that specific service is built and operated, not just on the road existing.

The two disciplines converge precisely because SRE can't realistically walk into every one of hundreds of teams and enforce standardized SLOs by persuasion alone. The leverage point is the platform itself: when SRE's reliability requirements get built directly into the platform's default templates — observability wired in automatically, a canary step in every pipeline, a standard SLO config shipped with every new service scaffold — standardization stops being something SRE enforces team by team and becomes something the platform hands every team for free.

That's directly a toil-reduction strategy too: baking a reliability default into the platform once removes a piece of manual, repetitive setup work that every team would otherwise have had to repeat for itself — exactly the definition of toil from the last lesson. When these teams don't collaborate, the failure mode is predictable: a paved road optimized purely for convenience with no reliability guardrails, and SRE stuck retrofitting observability onto services after the fact — expensive, inconsistent, and exactly the toil this chapter keeps naming as a problem.

Structurally, this usually looks like one of two things: a centralized platform team building the road with SRE as a close consulting partner embedding its requirements into the defaults, or a combined Platform SRE function owning both responsibilities outright. Either works. What doesn't work is treating them as unrelated. That closes Chapter 1 — dependency complexity, standardized SLO practice, error budgets as enforced policy, toil as a funded engineering priority, and SRE's real partnership with platform engineering all describe the same shift: reliability at enterprise scale runs on measured systems, not individual heroics.
